title: Revision on whole and natural numbers
competency: Describe whole and natural numbers and the relation between them.

keywords.def: A natural number or zero. 𝕎 = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.

en.text: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on. Whole numbers are the natural numbers together with 0. So every natural number is whole, but 0 is whole and not natural. There is no greatest natural or whole number.

screens.title: The biggest number?
screens.ask: What is the greatest natural number?
screens.after:
Add 1 to any natural number and you get a bigger one.
100 + 1 = 101. 1,000,000 + 1 = 1,000,001.
The list never ends, so there is no greatest natural number.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A natural number or zero. 𝕎 = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.

screens.text: Natural and whole numbers: what is the smallest whole number?
screens.why:
Whole numbers are 𝕎 = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.
The list starts at 0.
So the smallest whole number is 0.
1 is the smallest natural number, not the smallest whole number.
−1 is not a whole number at all.
screens.clue: Look at the first element of 𝕎.

screens.text: True or false? All whole numbers are natural numbers.
screens.why:
Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, …
0 is in the first list but not in the second.
So not all whole numbers are natural. False.

screens.text: Whole numbers: tap the first five whole numbers.
screens.why:
Whole numbers start at 0.
Count five of them: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
5 is the sixth whole number, so leave it out.

screens.ask: Count the natural numbers: how many natural numbers are less than 10? ___
screens.why:
Natural numbers start at 1.
Those less than 10 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
Count them: 9 numbers.
0 is not natural, and 10 is not less than 10.

en.text: Adding or multiplying two whole numbers always gives a whole number. Subtracting or dividing may not. For example 3 − 5 and 7 ÷ 2 are not whole numbers. That is why we need new numbers.

screens.title: Can we subtract?
screens.after:
3 − 5 asks: take 5 from 3.
Whole numbers stop at 0, so we run out after taking 3.
3 − 5 is not a whole number.
We need negative numbers for this. That is the topic of this unit.

screens.title: Note
paras: Adding or multiplying stays inside the set.
Subtracting or dividing can leave the set.
Tap each card below to see why.

screens.title: Which operations stay whole?
items: Natural + natural is always natural. Whole + whole is always whole. 4 + 0 = 4.
Natural × natural is always natural. Whole × whole is always whole. 3 × 0 = 0.
Not always natural, not always whole. 3 − 5 is neither.
Not always natural. 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 is not natural.

screens.clue: Add ones, then tens, then hundreds. Carry when needed.

screens.why:
Ones: 3 − 4 cannot be done. Borrow 1 ten: 13 − 4 = 9.
Tens: 4 − 1 = 3 tens left. 3 − 3 = 0.
Hundreds: 5 − 2 = 3.
Thousands: 6.
So 6543 − 234 = 6309. Check: 6309 + 234 = 6543.
screens.clue: Borrow from the tens when the ones are too small.

screens.why:
Step 1: do the bracket: 654 − 345.
Ones: 14 − 5 = 9 (borrow). Tens: 4 − 4 = 0. Hundreds: 6 − 3 = 3. So 309.
Step 2: 23 + 309 = 332.
So 23 + (654 − 345) = 332.

screens.text: True or false? The difference of any two whole numbers is always a whole number.
screens.why:
Try a small number minus a big one: 3 − 5.
We cannot take 5 from 3 and stay at 0 or above.
3 − 5 is not a whole number.
One example is enough to show the statement is false.
screens.clue: Try a small number minus a big one.

screens.text: Operations on whole numbers: which result is NOT a whole number?
screens.why:
Work out each one.
12 + 0 = 12, a whole number.
7 × 8 = 56, a whole number.
9 − 9 = 0, a whole number.
20 ÷ 8 = 2.5. It has a decimal part, so it is not whole.
Answer: 20 ÷ 8.

test.text: Natural numbers: which number is a natural number?
test.why:
Natural numbers are ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}.
7 is in this list, so 7 is natural.
0 is whole but not natural.
−2 is negative, so it is not natural.

test.text: True or false? 0 is a whole number.
test.why:
Whole numbers are 𝕎 = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.
The list starts with 0.
So 0 is a whole number. True.

Ones: 2 + 9 = 11. Write 1, carry 1.
Tens: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1.
Hundreds: 4 + 5 + 1 = 10.
So 452 + 589 = 1041.

900 has no ones or tens to take from. Borrow from the hundreds.
900 = 8 hundreds + 9 tens + 10 ones.
Ones: 10 − 7 = 3. Tens: 9 − 5 = 4. Hundreds: 8 − 4 = 4.
So 900 − 457 = 443. Check: 443 + 457 = 900.

test.text: Operations on whole numbers: the product of two whole numbers is
test.why:
Multiplying is repeated adding: 3 × 4 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Adding whole numbers always gives a whole number.
So the product of two whole numbers is always whole.
It is never negative: there are no negative whole numbers.
